result: Wild-type C. elegans hermaphrodites exhibit natural variability in Sh1 position, with bare regions (lacking somatic gonadal cell coverage) present between the DTC and Sh1 in the majority of gonads. This was confirmed using multiple imaging approaches including live confocal microscopy with various markers, TEM analysis, and antibody staining.
evaluation: Claims C33-C41 and C64 provide converging evidence from multiple independent methods (live imaging with multiple markers, TEM, antibody staining) demonstrating the existence of bare regions in wild-type animals. The quantitative data (70% Class 1 gonads, distances >25 µm) and consistency across methods strongly support this result.

result: Reduction of soma-germline gap-junctional activity through hypomorphic mutations in either germline innexin (inx-14(ag17)) or somatic innexins (inx-8(rf)) causes distal displacement of Sh1 towards the distal end of the gonad, greatly diminishing bare regions.
evaluation: Claims C5 and C43-C54 provide consistent quantitative evidence from multiple genetic backgrounds and imaging methods showing that reduced innexin function causes Sh1 to shift distally. The statistical significance of the shifts and consistency across different alleles and markers strongly support this conclusion.

result: The mKate2::INX-8 fusion protein encoded by inx-8(qy78[mKate2::inx-8]) acts as a dominant dosage-sensitive antimorph that causes distal mispositioning of Sh1. Deletion of the fusion protein by CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing restores normal Sh1 position and suppresses the phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C7, C48-C55, C68-C75, C80-C82, and C91-C96 provide strong genetic evidence including dosage analysis, deletion rescue experiments, and phenotypic characterization demonstrating the antimorphic nature of the fusion protein. The CRISPR deletion experiments provide particularly compelling evidence by showing phenotype suppression upon removal of the fusion.

result: Sh1 mispositioning does not markedly alter the position of the stem cell pool border as measured by SYGL-1 expression. Although the distal border of Sh1 shifts dramatically in innexin mutants, the proximal border of the SYGL-1-positive stem cell pool remains largely unchanged, and there is no significant correlation between Sh1 position and stem cell pool border position.
evaluation: Claims C8, C11, C86, C137, and C185-C190 provide quantitative data from SYGL-1 staining showing no significant correlation between Sh1 position and stem cell pool border across multiple genotypes. The use of SYGL-1 as a direct GLP-1/Notch target provides a robust readout of stem cell fate, and the statistical analysis (Pearson correlation) supports the lack of relationship.

result: Sh1 mispositioning does not markedly alter the position of the progenitor pool border. Although there is a modest but significant shortening of the progenitor zone in strains bearing mKate2::INX-8, this effect is very modest compared to the dramatic shift in Sh1 position, and there is no gonad-by-gonad correlation between Sh1 position and the progenitor zone border.
evaluation: Claims C9, C12, C143-C145, and C200-C204 provide quantitative data from CYE-1 staining showing that while there is a subtle effect on progenitor zone length in mKate2::INX-8 strains, this does not correlate with Sh1 position on an individual gonad basis. The lack of correlation and the modest effect size support the conclusion that Sh1 position does not dictate progenitor pool borders.

result: Gap junctions can control the position of Sh1 and contribute to the positioning of cells relative to each other in the context of the organ system, demonstrating a role for innexins in somatic gonad architecture.
evaluation: Claims C10, C90, and C163 are supported by the collective evidence showing that mutations affecting gap junction function consistently alter Sh1 position. The multiple genetic manipulations (hypomorphic alleles, antimorphic fusion protein) all converge on the same phenotype, strongly supporting a role for gap junctions in cell positioning.

result: Sh1 is not involved in the germline stem-progenitor fate decision. The position of Sh1 does not influence stem cell fate as measured by SYGL-1 expression, and if spindle-oriented divisions occur at the Sh1 border, they are not influencing stem cell fate.
evaluation: Claims C89, C153, C197, and C198 are supported by the experimental evidence showing no correlation between Sh1 position and stem cell pool borders across multiple genotypes. This directly tests and refutes the model proposed by Gordon et al., 2020, providing strong evidence against a role for Sh1 in stem cell fate decisions.

result: The finding that mKate2::INX-8 is a dominant antimorph resolves the apparent discrepancy in the literature concerning the anatomical position of Sh1. The fusion protein perturbs innexin function, causing distal mispositioning of Sh1 and obliterating bare regions, which led to an incorrect model in the prior study.
evaluation: Claims C97-C107 provide a coherent explanation for discrepancies in the literature by demonstrating that the mKate2::INX-8 fusion protein used in Gordon et al., 2020 is itself causing the phenotype it was used to observe. The confirmation of bare regions using multiple independent methods (TEM, antibody staining, multiple live markers) in unmarked strains strongly supports this resolution.

result: The lim-7 promoter-driven GFP markers (bcIs39, tnIs5, tnIs6) and other Sh1 markers (fasn-1(av138), acy-4(tnEx42)) reliably mark the distal extent of Sh1 despite some variability in expression. The overlap between these markers and mKate2::INX-8 is complete in the majority of gonads, and the markers consistently detect distal displacement of Sh1 in innexin mutants.
evaluation: Claims C58-C63 and C112-C116 address concerns about marker reliability by showing that multiple independent markers give consistent results and that the GFP markers can detect the distal shift of Sh1 in mutants. The quantitative data on marker overlap and the consistency across multiple markers support the reliability of these tools.

result: The model proposed by Gordon et al., 2020—that Sh1 guides oriented asymmetric divisions of stem cells and participates in a direct handoff of cells from the DTC to Sh1—is called into question by the current study's results showing that Sh1 position does not influence stem cell fate decisions.
evaluation: Claims C27-C32, C101, and C151 describe the prior model and the current study's refutation of it. The experimental evidence showing no correlation between Sh1 position and stem cell borders, combined with the finding that the prior model was based on an antimorphic marker, strongly supports the rejection of this model.

result: The position of Sh1 is sensitive to the dosage of somatic gap junction hemichannels, as evidenced by the observation of Class 3 gonads in inx-8 deletion heterozygotes and the haploinsufficient behavior of inx-8(qy78tn2031)/+.
evaluation: Claims C76, C77, and C84 provide genetic evidence for dosage sensitivity through analysis of heterozygotes. The observation of Class 3 gonads in deletion heterozygotes but not wild-type, and the haploinsufficient phenotype, support the conclusion that Sh1 position is sensitive to innexin dosage.

result: Brood size analysis shows that the bcIs39 marker alone does not significantly affect brood size compared to wild-type. However, there is a discrepancy in embryonic lethality measurements between the current study (~1%) and Li et al., 2022 (~20%) for the same strain, which might reflect variations in growth conditions or genetic drift.
evaluation: Claims C154-C157 and C159 present conflicting observations between studies without a clear resolution. While the current study provides quantitative data showing no significant difference in brood size with the marker, the discrepancy in embryonic lethality remains unexplained. The speculative explanations (growth conditions, genetic drift) are not tested.

result: The study addresses concerns raised by Li et al., 2022 about the utility of bcIs39[lim-7p::ced-1::gfp] as a marker for Sh1, showing that while there is some variability in expression (15-20% of gonads), this variability is not biologically meaningful and the marker reliably detects the distal extent of Sh1.
evaluation: Claims C110-C123 provide a detailed response to methodological concerns from a prior study. The quantitative data on marker overlap, the consistency of results across multiple markers, and the ability to detect Sh1 displacement in mutants support the reliability of the markers despite some variability.

result: The study hypothesizes that membrane-associated Sh1 markers described by Li et al., 2022 (CAM-1::mNeonGreen, INA-1::mNeonGreen, lim-7p::GFP::CAAX) may similarly disrupt functions that act to position Sh1, displaying reduced or absent bare regions, but this hypothesis is not tested in the current study.
evaluation: Claims C127-C131 present a hypothesis about why other markers show discordant results, but this hypothesis is explicitly stated as beyond the scope of the current study and is not experimentally tested. The speculation is reasonable given the findings with mKate2::INX-8, but lacks direct evidence.

result: The biological significance of bare regions remains uncertain. While loss of bare regions correlates with only a modest effect on brood size, the innexins have multiple functions in germline development, making it difficult to ascribe the brood-size reduction specifically to the absence of bare regions.
evaluation: Claims C160-C162 acknowledge a limitation of the study in determining the functional significance of bare regions. The modest effect on brood size and the multiple functions of innexins make it difficult to draw definitive conclusions about the role of bare regions, and the authors appropriately note that additional study is required.

result: The study proposes several speculative mechanisms for how gap junctions might control Sh1 position, including roles in adhesion, channel function, and dynamic association/dissociation with germ cells. However, these mechanisms are not directly tested and remain speculative.
evaluation: Claims C164-C183 present various hypotheses and speculations about the mechanisms underlying gap junction control of Sh1 position. While these are reasonable hypotheses based on the data and prior literature, they are explicitly speculative and not experimentally tested in the current study. The discussion appropriately acknowledges the complexity of disentangling adhesive and channel functions.

result: The current study directly tests the model that Sh1 influences the stem cell border by altering Sh1 position and assaying SYGL-1 expression, in contrast to Li et al., 2022 which used indirect proxies. The findings are consistent with other observations in the literature showing that stem cell pools exist in males (which lack sheath cells) and in larval stages before DTC process elaboration.
evaluation: Claims C132-C150 describe the experimental approach and its consistency with prior literature. The use of SYGL-1 as a direct GLP-1/Notch target provides a more robust test of the model than indirect proxies, and the consistency with observations in males and larval stages strengthens the conclusion that Sh1 position does not dictate stem cell fate.

result: The study validates its visual assessment of SYGL-1 zone length by showing that the visually determined border consistently corresponds to 6-9% of peak SYGL-1 intensity across genotypes. In wild-type, the distal border of Sh1 is proximal to the SYGL-1 border in 86% of gonads, with a distance ≥5 cell diameters in 67% of gonads, which is inconsistent with a model of Sh1 controlling spindle orientation at the stem cell border.
evaluation: Claims C191-C196 provide quantitative validation of the SYGL-1 measurement method and demonstrate that the spatial relationship between Sh1 and the stem cell border is inconsistent with the proposed model. The quantitative data and statistical analysis support these conclusions.

result: Analysis of the progenitor zone border using CYE-1 and pSUN-1 co-staining shows that Sh1 position is variable in wild-type and can be either distal or proximal to the PZ border. Although there is a subtle shift in the PZ border in innexin mutants, it does not correlate with the dramatic shift in Sh1 position, and the relationships are similar whether measurements are made in microns or cell diameters.
evaluation: Claims C199-C202 provide quantitative data on the relationship between Sh1 position and the progenitor zone border. The lack of correlation between Sh1 position and PZ border, despite dramatic shifts in Sh1 position in mutants, supports the conclusion that Sh1 position does not dictate the PZ border.

result: The study provides a cautionary tale that fusion proteins used as markers, even when generated by genome editing of the endogenous locus, may not be benign and can perturb the biological processes they are intended to observe.
evaluation: Claims C108 and C109 draw a general conclusion from the specific findings about mKate2::INX-8. The demonstration that an endogenously tagged fusion protein can act as an antimorph provides an important cautionary example for the field, supported by the detailed genetic and phenotypic characterization.
